title: Checkmate the Sphinx
reviewNotes: Two branches, 10 exact positions from the supported seven-piece source diagram after a6 ...bxa6 at 66s. Earlier eight-piece pawn offer remains context. Kc2 h2 Be5 ...h1=Q Nc3+ leads to Bc7 mate after ...Ka5 or Bd6 mate after ...Kxa3. The capture of White’s a3 pawn is preserved.
transcript: The Sphinx gives you this position, and she tells you that she's going to let you live and proceed in the labyrinth if you can checkmate her with white from this position. At first glance, it might seem like this is going to be an easy task. We have a bishop and a knight left, and black is only left with two pawns, but this pawn here in particular is a pretty big problem because it's only one step away from promoting to a new queen, and unfortunately, it seems like every piece is too slow to reach that pawn. The pawn can simply [music] promote in time, and there is no mating net around this king. If we try to make the knight, now the pawn is simply going to push, and after this check, the king is simply able to take this pawn and run free. So, it almost seems like the Sphinx is trying to mock us, and there is no solution to this position. But actually, there is a way to checkmate black, and we have to start with the last move that you could possibly think of in this position. We are going to play a6. Now, giving up a pawn seemingly for free. Of course, if this pawn ignores us, now we are also going to run [music] and get our queen in time with a check, meaning that this is going to be an easy win. But the Sphinx laughs and simply takes the pawn. There's nothing here, right? Maybe not yet. But follow me here. We are going to be playing king to c2. Another seemingly ridiculous and pointless move. The Sphinx pushes the pawn, and it's only one square away >> [music] >> from getting that queen. But this is where our plan is going to unfold because actually, we can indeed stop the pawn with the brilliant >> [music] >> bishop e5. A very precise move that does two things at the same time. The first thing is obvious. This attacks the pawn, but it seems like black can simply get a new queen anyway and get out of the attack. But we're going to follow up this plan with knight to c3 check, and now we start to see the idea behind sacrificing the pawn. If the king comes up to a5, out of nowhere, bishop c7 would be a checkmate. The pawn plays a key role in stopping his own king from escaping. And if the king comes down, this is yet another checkmate after Bishop to D6. We checkmate the Sphinx and we're going to continue exploring this labyrinth.
